items.title: US Department of Labor announces final rule clarifying employee, independent contractor status under federal wage and hour laws
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. The new final rule provides clarity to businesses and workers alike, as well as the division’s enforcement personnel.U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Wage and Hour Division Administrator Andrew Rogers, and other department officials hosted an event to formally announce the final rule at the Frances Perkins Building this morning. Employers, business associations, worker advocates, independent contractors, and other stakeholders were in attendance as Secretary Sonderling highlighted the clarity and simplicity of the new regulations.The final rule rescinds an earlier 2024 rule addressing the classification of employees and independent contractors and replaces it with an analysis that is substantially similar to the framework adopted by the department in 2021. Consistent with the outcomes of federal appellate cases, the final rule provides further guidance on the process for differentiating between employees with protections under the FLSA and individuals who work as independent contractors.“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” said Secretary Sonderling. “The new Independent Contractor final rule establishes clear, predictable, and easy-to-understand criteria for determining who is an employee and who is an independent contractor – allowing millions of Americans to take advantage of new opportunities in President Trump’s booming economy.”The final rule also applies the department’s streamlined analysis to the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, both of which use the FLSA’s statutory definition of “employ.” However, the rule does not chan
items.content_html: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. The new final rule provides clarity to businesses and workers alike, as well as the division’s enforcement personnel.U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Wage and Hour Division Administrator Andrew Rogers, and other department officials hosted an event to formally announce the final rule at the Frances Perkins Building this morning. Employers, business associations, worker advocates, independent contractors, and other stakeholders were in attendance as Secretary Sonderling highlighted the clarity and simplicity of the new regulations.The final rule rescinds an earlier 2024 rule addressing the classification of employees and independent contractors and replaces it with an analysis that is substantially similar to the framework adopted by the department in 2021. Consistent with the outcomes of federal appellate cases, the final rule provides further guidance on the process for differentiating between employees with protections under the FLSA and individuals who work as independent contractors.“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” said Secretary Sonderling. “The new Independent Contractor final rule establishes clear, predictable, and easy-to-understand criteria for determining who is an employee and who is an independent contractor – allowing millions of Americans to take advantage of new opportunities in President Trump’s booming economy.”The final rule also applies the department’s streamlined analysis to the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, both of which use the FLSA’s statutory definition of “employ.” However, the rule does not change the assessment of employee or independent contractor status for the purpose of any other federal laws, including the Internal Revenue Code, and does not preempt any state or local laws.“The Department of Labor is committed to helping employers prevent misclassification. This rule strikes the right balance by protecting employees who are entitled to the protections of federal wage and hour laws, while also respecting the entrepreneurial spirit of legitimate independent contractors,” said Administrator Rogers. “The department distilled longstanding judicial tests into a framework that employees and employers can reliably apply at the outset of business relationships.”The analysis in the department’s final rule does the following:Applies an “economic reality” test to determine whether a worker is in business for himself or herself as an independent contractor or is an employee economically dependent on an employer for work.Identifies and explains two “core factors” to help determine if a worker is economically dependent on an employer for work or in business for himself or herself:The nature and degree of control over the work.The worker’s opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative and/or investment.Identifies other factors to help determine a worker’s status as an employee or independent contractor, including the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.Advises that the actual practice of the worker and the potential employer is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible.Provides 14 fact-specific examples applying the factors to real-life circumstances. The department published a notice of proposed rulemaking on Feb. 27, 2026, and received approximately 16,500 public comments during a 60-day comment period. After reviewing this feedback, the department finalized the rule with modifications and enhancements. For example, in response to commenter requests, the final rule includes new illustrative examples involving farm labor contractors, digital platform workers, and truck drivers.Workers and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the FMLA.WATCH the Independent Contractor Final Rule Announcement.Read Secretary Sonderling’s Op-Ed on the Final Rule.Read the final rule, which takes effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

items.title: US Department of Labor obtains court order requiring NJ-based  construction contractor to pay $2.2M in back wages, damages, penalties
items.content_text: ENGLEWOOD CLIFFS, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a construction contractor to pay more than $2 million in back wages and damages to 323 construction workers.     Entered Nov. 16, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, the consent judgment resolves the department’s litigation alleging Premier Concrete Systems LLC and its owners, Peter Tiflinsky and Antonio Escada, violated overtime and recordkeeping provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.The litigation was a result of an investigation by the department’s Wage and Hour Division that found the company and its owners paid employees cash at straight-time rates for all hours worked and failed to pay them time and one-half their regular rate of pay for hours over 40 in a workweek as required by the FLSA. “Construction workers play a critical role across the country in ensuring safe and reliable structures. The Wage and Hour Division is committed to ensuring that construction workers are paid in compliance with federal labor laws,” said Wage and Hour Division Regional Administrator James Cain in Philadelphia.The judgment requires Premier Concrete Systems to pay 323 employees back wages totaling $1,040,648 and an equal amount in damages. The judgment also requires the defendants to pay a civil penalty of $118,704 and prohibits defendants from violating the FLSA in the future.“The resolution of this case is a clear reminder for employers in the construction industry to remember their responsibilities under the law,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

items.title: US Department of Labor issues opinion letters addressing Fair Labor Standards Act exemption, Family and Medical Leave Act hours of service
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today issued two opinion letters that address real-world questions related to the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Family and Medical Leave Act.The two opinion letters address the applicability of the exemption for amusement and recreational establishments under the Fair Labor Standards Act and the hours-of-service requirement under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Opinion letters provide official written interpretations from the department’s Wage and Hour Division that explain how the laws that the department enforces apply to specific factual circumstances and may help the public understand their rights and responsibilities. The division is committed to providing opinion letters that help American workers and businesses understand how the FLSA and FMLA apply to their situations.   The two opinion letters issued today are:FLSA2026-14: Whether the exemption for seasonal amusement and recreational establishments in section 13(a)(3) of the FLSA applies to a concessionaire that provides food and drinks at events such as a state fair and concerts.FMLA2026-3: Whether time spent writing mandatory reports outside of scheduled work hours and traveling between worksites counts as hours of service under the FMLA. In 2025, the department announced the relaunch of the opinion letter program, which expands its longstanding commitment to providing meaningful compliance assistance that helps workers, employers, and other stakeholders understand how federal labor laws apply in specific workplace circumstances.Visit the Wage and Hour Division’s opinion letters page to explore past guidance and find information on how to submit a request for an opinion letter.Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits

items.title: US Department of Labor applauds federal appeals court decision on administrative exhaustion requirement under federal benefits law
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor applauded a federal appeals court decision allowing employees to bring legal claims directly to federal court if they reasonably suspect fiduciary violations in their employee benefit plans covered under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.Issued Oct. 13 by the en banc 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, the unanimous decision in Bolton v. Inland Fresh Seafood overturns precedent that required employees to exhaust all administrative remedies under their ERISA-covered employee benefit plans before they could go to federal court. “This decision vindicates the department’s reinvigorated amicus program and its focus on statutory text,” said Solicitor of Labor Jonathan Berry. “ERISA neither explicitly nor implicitly requires hard-working Americans to go anywhere but federal court to vindicate their statutory rights under it. By overruling its precedent that erroneously held otherwise, the 11th Circuit joins all but one of its sister circuits and reinforces ERISA’s uniform statutory framework.”The court held that the exhaustion requirement was not based on ERISA’s text, saying it was an “atextual product of judicial creation based solely on policy reasons.” The court’s opinion also quoted the department’s oral argument, saying “plaintiffs or employers should not be able to contract away or force their employees to contract away their rights under ERISA.” “The decision by the 11th Circuit rightly rejects a judicially invented exhaustion requirement that has no basis in ERISA’s text or Congressional intent,” said Assistant Secretary of Labor for the Employee Benefits Security Administration Daniel Aronowitz. “By aligning with the law’s clear text and Congress's intent to provide participants and beneficiaries direct access to federal court, the court’s decision makes certain that ERISA’s protections are applied as written in the statute itself.”Employers and workers can contact EBSA at askebsa.dol.gov or call 866-444-3272 to

[November 9, 2026]
 PER CURIAM. 
Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immi-
grant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secre-
tary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct bor-
der barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of 
high illegal entry into the United States.”  §102(a), 110 Stat.
3009–554, as amended, note following 8 U. S. C. §1103.  The 
same section expressly authorizes the Secretary “ ‘to waive
all legal requirements’ ” as “ ‘necessary to ensure expedi-
tious construction’ ” of those barriers and roads, §102(c)(1),
119 Stat. 306, and sharply limits judicial review of all 
claims arising from such waiver determinations.  Specifi -
cally, the statute provides that “‘[a] cause of action or claim 
may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution
of the United States’ ” and courts “ ‘shall not have jurisdic-
tion’” over nonconstitutional claims.  §102(c)(2)(A).
Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102’s
waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at 
the U. S.–Mexico border, in a region that U. S. Customs and 
Border Protection has designated the “Big Bend Sector.”
The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector “is an area of
high illegal entry” requiring additional border barriers, and 
waived the application of a variety of environmental and 
conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

The Judicial Branch experienced an email outage on Thursday, November 12, 2026 that began at approximately 1:00 p.m. and lasted through Friday, November 13, 2026 at approximately 7:00 a.m. The Judicial Branch's email outage was part of the larger Microsoft Outlook outage that spread throughout North America.

Judicial Branch Issues Amendment to Administrative Order on the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS), Effective November 2, 2026
Date:
11/2/2026
The Maine Judicial Branch announced today that an Administrative Order on rules and procedures applicable to Maine eCourts and eFiling has been amended regarding the use of non-Judicial Branch court forms when one has been provided by the court.
AO JB 20-03 (A. 11-26)
was adopted in 2020 to provide guidance on the applicability of the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) during the transitional period during the implementation of Maine eCourts and electronic filing when there are conflicts between MRECS and other Judicial Branch rules and administrative orders.
New Section I.C. of JB 20-20 provides that "[i]f an applicable court-approved form exists and is available to the public, the parties must use it" and further adds the following requirement:
"If a filer does not use a form, the filer must include a brief explanation in a cover letter accompanying the submission that indicates the existing form is not suitable."
Barbara Cardone, Director of Legal Affairs and Public Relations explained the reason for the amendment. "The reason for the amendment is to increase the efficiency of reviewing eFiling submissions. eFilers who submit non-Judicial Branch-approved court forms can avoid having their submission rejected by including an explanatory cover letter with the eFiling. We hope this clarification helps the eFiling and legal community's smooth transition to eFiling and Maine eCourts."
AO JB 20-03 (A. 11-26) has been posted on the Administrative Orders page of the Judicial Branch website at
https://www.courts.maine.gov/adminorders/index.html
Supporting documents

Judicial Branch Announces Procedure for Emergency Case Filings Regarding Elections
Date:
10/29/2026
AUGUSTA, Maine. The Maine Judicial Branch announced the procedure for emergency case filings regarding elections to be held on November 3, 2026.
Procedure for Election Filings
In order to expedite the review of filings, Superior Court Chief Justice Robert Mullen and District Court Chief Judge Brent Davis issued a
standing order on October 28th
requiring
all filings pertaining to the November 3 election and filed between Friday, October 30, 2026, at 4:00 pm and Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 9:00 pm to be filed on paper at the clerk's office.  Filers should NOT use the eFile Maine system
for these emergency filings.
Filings submitted on paper will be reviewed immediately by a clerk and can be directed to the appropriate justice for timely review.  Filers are also encouraged to put their cell phone numbers or emergency telephone numbers (where they can be reached after hours) on their filings.
State Courts Open Late on November 3
The state courthouses in Bangor, Augusta and Portland will be open until 9:00 p.m. for the purpose of accepting and acting on emergency paper filings regarding elections.  A judge, a clerk and a marshal will be on duty at each courthouse.
Availability of Documents to the Media
All public documents related to election filings will be posted on the high-profile page of the Judicial Branchs public website as soon as is practicable.
Supporting documents

items.title: Standing Order: Standing Order Requiring Paper Filing for Election Day 2026 Emergency Matters
items.content_text:
STATE OF MAINE       SUPERIOR COURT 
DISTRICT COURT 
 
  
STANDING ORDER REQUIRING 
PAPER FILING FOR ELECTION DAY 
2026 EMERGENCY MATTERS 
 
 
 The Maine Judicial Branch (MJB) is implementing the Maine eCourts 
system – including eFiling – statewide.1  EFileMaine is a practical and efficient 
document submission system already in use in many courts throughout the 
state.  However, because filings related to Election Day may be uniquely time-
sensitive, to ensure timely processing, the MJB will require paper filing under 
the limited circumstances described below.   
 
 It is therefore ORDERED that any emergency Title 21-A filings related to 
Election Day 2026 filed between 4:00 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, and 
9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, must be by paper, unless otherwise 
ordered.2 
 
It is further ORDERED that the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems 
are SUSPENDED to the extent necessary to give effect to this order.   
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   _____/s/______________________   
       Chief Justice Robert E. Mullen 
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   ___/s/_______________________   
       Chief Judge Brent Davis 
 
1 Further information about the Maine eCourts system is available at 
https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html 
2 Any Election Day 2026 filings filed by eFile during this period may not be processed until the next business 
day after the election.

items.title: Seal Cove Auto Museum v. John J. Sanford et al.
items.content_text:
MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT Reporter of Decisions 
Decision:  2026 ME 110 
Docket: BCD-25-555 
Argued: October 8, 2026 
Decided:  November 19, 2026 
 
Panel:  STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, CONNORS, DOUGLAS, and LIPEZ, JJ.  
 
 
SEAL COVE AUTO MUSEUM 
 
v. 
 
JOHN J. SANFORD et al. 
 
 
LIPEZ, J. 
[¶1]  In 2020, the parties to this appeal, Seal Cove Auto Museum , the 
Richard C. Paine, Jr., Automobile Collection Charitable Trust  (the Trust or the 
Charitable Trust), and the Trust’s trustees, John J. Sanford and John  Peabody 
Monks Higgins (the Trustees) , entered into a settlement agreement and an 
amended relationship agreement to resolve a legal dispute.  In 2022, after the 
Trust announced a plan to donate $1,000,000 to the Owls Head Transportation 
Museum, Seal Cove filed a motion to enforce, arguing that the donation to Owls 
Head violated the Trust’s and the Trustees’ obligations under the agreements.  
After a bench trial, t he Business and Consumer Docket ( Duddy, J.) denied the 
motion, and Seal Cove now appeals, primarily asserting  that the trial court 
misinterpreted relevant provisions of the amended relationship agreement and 
 
 
2 
erred in finding that the Trust had not breached that agreement.  Upon review 
of Seal Cove’s arguments, we conclude that they lack merit, and we accordingly 
affirm. 
I.  BACKGROUND 
 [¶2]  This is not the first time that we have addressed an appeal involving 
these parties.  As we explained in Attorney General v. Sanford: 
Richard Paine Jr. established Seal Cove in 1963 and the 
Richard C. Paine, Jr., Automobile Collection Charitable Trust (the 
Trust) in 1986.  The Trust and Seal Cove were established to 
maintain and display Paine ’s large collection of antique 
automobiles.  Following Paine's death in 2007, the Trust acquired 
most of Paine ’s automobiles and an endowment to support 
maintenance and display of the automobile collection.  Sanford and 
Higgins presently serve as trustees of the Trust. 
 
. . . The Declara
